title: Rectangle Sums on a Table That Changes

concept.title: A Fenwick tree of Fenwick trees: the same lowest-bit jumps in both coordinates
body: A table of `h` rows and `w` columns starts with zeros. Operations **add a number to one cell** and questions ask for the **sum of the cells in a rectangle**. For a 3 by 3 table with 5 added to the cell (2, 2) and 7 to the cell (3, 1), the rectangle of the rows 2 to 3 and the columns 1 to 2 has the sum 12. Summing the rectangle cell by cell is O(h w) per question.

The one-dimensional Fenwick tree extends to two dimensions: `T[i][j]` stores the sum of the rectangle of the rows `i - lowbit(i) + 1 .. i` and the columns `j - lowbit(j) + 1 .. j`. To **add** to the cell (r, c), update every `T[i][j]` with `i` going up from `r` by `i += i & -i` and, inside, `j` going up from `c`. To get the **prefix rectangle** sum `S(r, c)` of the rows `1..r` and the columns `1..c`, go down in both coordinates with `i -= i & -i` and `j -= j & -j`. A rectangle is the usual inclusion-exclusion of four prefix rectangles.

Each operation takes O(log h * log w) steps (about 80 for a 500 by 500 table), and the memory is O(h w). For a rectangle query four prefix sums are needed, so about 300 steps. The 2D tree is the standard structure for "count points in a rectangle" with online updates.

statement: A table with `h` rows and `w` columns contains zeros. Process `q` operations: type 1 `r c x 0` adds `x` to the cell in the row `r` and the column `c`; type 2 `r1 c1 r2 c2` asks for the sum of the cells in the rows `r1` to `r2` and the columns `c1` to `c2`. Print the answers to the questions on one line, in order.
inputFormat: The first line has `h`, `w` and `q`: the height and the width of the table and the number of operations.

Each of the next `q` lines has five numbers `t`, `a`, `b`, `c` and `d`. If `t = 1`, add `c` to the cell in the row `a` and the column `b` (`d` is 0). If `t = 2`, print the sum of the cells in the rows `a` to `c` and the columns `b` to `d`.
outputFormat: Print one number for every operation of type 2, separated by spaces.
constraints: The table is all zeros at the start.
For a question 1 <= a <= c <= h and 1 <= b <= d <= w.

examples.note: The rectangle of the rows 2..3 and the columns 1..2 holds 5 and 7: 12. The whole table holds 12 as well: 12 12.

hints: Use a Fenwick tree inside a Fenwick tree.
An addition walks up in both coordinates; a prefix sum walks down in both.
A rectangle is S(r2, c2) - S(r1 - 1, c2) - S(r2, c1 - 1) + S(r1 - 1, c1 - 1).

import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

h, w, q = map(int, input().split())
ops = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(q)]

# Your code here

explanation: A two-dimensional Fenwick tree stores partial rectangle sums; an addition updates the cells reached by the lowest-bit jumps in both coordinates, and a rectangle sum combines four prefix rectangles.
solution.complexity: Time O(q log h log w), space O(h w).

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

h, w, q = map(int, input().split())
ops = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(q)]

T = [[0] * (w + 1) for _ in range(h + 1)]

def prefix(r, c):
    s = 0
    i = r
    while i > 0:
        row = T[i]
        j = c
        while j > 0:
            s += row[j]
            j -= j & -j
        i -= i & -i
    return s

out = []
for kind, a, b, c, d in ops:
    if kind == 1:
        i = a
        while i <= h:
            row = T[i]
            j = b
            while j <= w:
                row[j] += c
                j += j & -j
            i += i & -i
    else:
        out.append(prefix(c, d) - prefix(a - 1, d) - prefix(c, b - 1) + prefix(a - 1, b - 1))
print(*out)
